big: Compliance feels like paperwork until the day a client says "you told me it was safe". Four habits protect your ARN and a client list built over twenty years: disclose, profile, make no promises, and show the riskometer.

lines: Will this fund definitely give me 12%? My neighbour's adviser said his fund would.
That sentence ends careers. Let us see what an answer looks like that is both compliant and genuinely helpful.

h: Can I say this to a client?
alt: A shield with statements that are safe to say and statements that are not
caps: What you say is part of the product. Compliance is a habit of words.
Say that returns are not assured, and say what you earn from the fund.
Never promise a return, and never imply the past will repeat.
title: Can I say this to a client?
stops: Returns are not assured on this fund
My trail commission on it is X% a year
It is safe, you will get 12%
It gave 18%, so expect that again

alt: Three bars on a six-step risk scale showing a client's comfort level and the risk level of two funds
caps: SEBI's riskometer has six levels, from Low to Very High. Meena's profile says Moderate.
Fund G is rated Moderate. It sits inside her comfort.
Fund F is rated Very High, three steps beyond what she said she can bear.
Show scheme and benchmark riskometers. A gap needs a different fund, not a different profile.

alt: Bars comparing the first-year cost and the value after fifteen years for a direct plan and a regular plan
caps: Same portfolio, ₹10 lakh for 15 years at 12% before costs. The costs are assumed for illustration.
A regular plan at 1.6% a year includes the distributor's commission. A direct plan at 0.8% does not.
After 15 years the gap is about ₹5 lakh. Clients will ask about this, so be ready to answer.
Say what you earn and what you do for it. Hiding it costs more than the commission ever did.

q: A client asks: "Do you earn anything if I buy this fund?" You receive a trail commission from the fund house. What is the right response?
opts: Tell him the trail commission, and what service it covers
Say the fund house pays, so it is not his concern
Reply that commissions are confidential between you and the AMC
Move to the direct plan topic without saying what you earn
why: Disclosure answers the question and lets him weigh your advice. Linking it to the service shows what he gets for it.
The fund house pays out of the fund's expense, which the client bears through the unit price, so it is his concern.
Distributors are expected to disclose commissions to clients. Calling them confidential hides what he has a right to know.
Talking about direct plans without answering is evasion. It looks like hiding the figure he asked for, and it erodes trust.

q: A retired client says: "Just tell me it will give 10% so I can sleep." Which reply is compliant and still useful?
opts: It has given about 10% before, so you can expect it again
It is a Moderate-risk fund, so 10% is a fair figure to rely on
A fund this old has a record, so the 10% is as good as fixed
I cannot promise 10%; let us check risk against your needs
why: Quoting past returns as an expectation implies the past will repeat. That is a form of assured return, which is not allowed.
A riskometer rating describes risk, not a return. Giving 10% as a figure to rely on still implies an assured return.
A long record is not a guarantee. Calling a return as good as fixed breaks the rule against implying assured returns.
It declines to promise, and turns his need for comfort into a check of what risk he can truly carry. Honest and helpful.

q: Meena's profile says Moderate. A fund you like carries a Very High riskometer. What do you do?
opts: Recommend it, since a small share makes the riskometer moot
Choose a fund within her profile and show both riskometers
Raise her risk profile to Very High so that the fund fits
Mention the riskometer only if she asks about it first
why: A small share still carries Very High risk. Suitability asks whether the product fits her, whatever the portion.
It starts from her profile, and showing scheme and benchmark riskometers lets her see the risk before she decides.
Changing a profile to fit a product is misselling. The profile must reflect what she can really bear, not what suits the sale.
The riskometer is part of every recommendation, not an optional extra. Waiting to be asked leaves out a required disclosure.

q: A client reading the new documents asks why costs now show a base expense ratio plus brokerage and taxes. What helps him most?
opts: Tell him the split is technical and he need not worry
Quote only the base ratio, as it is the lower figure
Show the base ratio and the added charges, then the total
Compare the new base ratio with old total ratios to show savings
why: Brushing it off leaves him uninformed. Under the 2026 rules cost transparency is higher, and clients will ask for a clear answer.
The base ratio alone understates what he pays, because brokerage and taxes sit outside it. Quoting only that misleads him.
Showing each part and the total gives him the full cost, and lets him compare funds like for like.
Old total ratios and the new base ratio measure different things, so comparing them can suggest savings that may not exist.

pts: Disclose what you earn, and recommend only after a risk profile. Change the fund, never the profile.
Never promise or imply an assured return on a market-linked product. Past returns are history, not a forecast.
Show scheme and benchmark riskometers. Costs now appear in parts, so be ready to explain each one clearly.
